explanations.explanation: Jeshua son of Jozadak, a priest, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel began to build the altar of the God of Israel. They did it to sacrifice burnt offerings on it, "as it is written in the Law of Moses the man of God." So the first thing going up is the place where the offerings will go. I like a crew that starts with what matters most, friend.

A wall is a solid idea, and I get why it comes to mind. But this passage never mentions a wall. It says Jeshua, Zerubbabel and their people began to build the altar. Burnt offerings were the plan, so the altar goes up first.

Good instinct, friend. If I'd heard the neighbors were scary, I'd be ordering a watchtower too, and a very small helmet for my hat. But no watchtower shows up in this passage. The text says they began to build the altar, and that's what they build.

That's the word. They set up the altar and sacrificed burnt offerings on it, both morning and evening, "even though they feared the people of the land." The fear is there, and so are the offerings. The text doesn't say the fear went away, only that they kept offering anyway.

Nice try, but trust isn't the word in this verse. The text says they offered the morning and evening burnt offerings even though they feared the people of the land. That "even though" tells you something was weighing on them. They kept offering anyway.

I can see why you'd pick it, since it sounds like a tough crowd. But the text says they feared the people of the land, and it doesn't say they ignored them. Fear and keeping on go together here. They set up the altar and offered the morning and evening burnt offerings all the same.
That's the one. The people "celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles in accordance with what is written." They weren't making up a holiday on the spot. They followed what was already written down.

The Feast of Weeks is a real feast in the Law, but it's not the one this verse names. Ezra 3:4 says they celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles, in accordance with what is written. This all happens in the seventh month, and that's the feast the text gives us.

Passover is a big one, so I see why it came to mind. But it's not the feast this verse names. The text says they celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles in accordance with what is written. Passover just isn't mentioned in this passage.

True. The text says they offered burnt offerings daily, "based on the number prescribed for each day." Nobody was winging it with the count. They followed what was written for every single day of the feast.

This one is actually true, friend. The verse says they offered burnt offerings daily "based on the number prescribed for each day." So the offerings were every day, and the number was already set. Nobody had to guess how many to bring.

This one's a sneaky one. The text says the Israelites began to offer burnt offerings on the first day of the seventh month, "although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid." So the answer is False. The offerings started first, and the foundation came later.

Right, it's False. The verse says the offerings began "although the foundation of the temple of the LORD had not been laid." So the altar was already working while the temple was still just a plan. Offerings first, foundation later.
Sea is right. The cedar logs came from Lebanon to Joppa by sea. The people of Sidon and Tyre were the ones bringing them. That's a lot of wood on the water, friend.

A camel is a good thought, but it's not what the verse says. The text says the cedar logs came from Lebanon to Joppa by sea. I'd pay good money to see a camel try to carry that load, though, hump and all.
A wagon makes sense if you're picturing a road. But the text says the logs came from Lebanon to Joppa by sea. The people of Sidon and Tyre were bringing them. So the route was water, not wheels.

It's actually False. The verse says they sent the cedar logs "as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia." Cyrus ruled Persia and was the one who sent the exiles home. So the Israelites had his go-ahead for the shipment.
Right, False. The cedar came "as authorized by Cyrus king of Persia." The Israelites weren't going around the king. They had his go-ahead for the shipment.

explanations.answer: Levites twenty years old and up
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says they appointed Levites twenty years of age or older to supervise the construction of the house of the LORD. Then Jeshua, Kadmiel, the sons of Henadad and their families joined together to supervise the workers. All of them were Levites.

Elders are a fine choice for a big project, but they're not who this verse names. The text says they appointed Levites twenty years of age or older to supervise the construction. The Levite families named in the next verse join in too.

Tyre does show up in this passage, so I see where that came from. But the text doesn't mention a Hiram. The people of Sidon and Tyre bring cedar logs, and the supervisors are Levites twenty years of age or older.

Yes. The priests with trumpets and the Levites with cymbals took their positions "to praise the LORD." The text says it was as David king of Israel had prescribed. A foundation was in, and the music was ready.
Trumpets can sound like a work whistle, I'll give you that. But the text says they took their positions to praise the LORD. The foundation was already laid, so this wasn't a call back to work.

Trumpets do sound like an alarm, so I see the thought. But this verse says they took their positions to praise the LORD, with no word of enemies coming. The foundation had just been laid, and the cymbals and trumpets were for praise.

That's the word. "Then all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid." It came right after the song, "For He is good; for His loving devotion to Israel endures forever." The whole crowd joined in.

A feast was earlier in the passage, so I see why it stuck. But in this moment the text says all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD. The foundation had been laid, and the crowd let it ring out.

Offerings do fill up this passage, so that's an easy one to grab. But here the text says all the people gave a great shout of praise to the LORD. It happened because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid.

explanations.answer: Older leaders who saw the first temple
explanations.explanation: That's them. "Many of the older priests, Levites, and family heads who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple." The text doesn't tell us exactly why they wept. I think those tears carried a lot, and I'll leave it at that.

explanations.answer: The people of Sidon and Tyre
explanations.explanation: Sidon and Tyre are in this passage, but they're the ones bringing cedar logs. The weeping comes from the older priests, Levites and family heads who had seen the first temple. The text puts the tears on them.

The people of the land do show up earlier, since the Israelites feared them. But they aren't the ones weeping at the foundation. Those tears came from the older priests, Levites and family heads who had seen the first temple.
True. The text says that while the older ones wept, "many others shouted joyfully." So the crowd had both sounds going at once, and it all happened at the same foundation.
It's actually True. The verse says the older leaders wept loudly, "Still, many others shouted joyfully." So tears and shouts were both going up in the same crowd at the same time.

explanations.answer: Tell the shouts of joy from the weeping
explanations.explanation: Yes. The text says "The people could not distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were making so much noise." Joyful shouts and loud weeping were so mixed together that nobody could sort them out. That's a loud crowd.

explanations.answer: See the foundation through the crowd
explanations.explanation: Good guess for a big crowd. But the text doesn't say anyone couldn't see the foundation. What they couldn't do was distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were making so much noise.

explanations.answer: Finish singing the song they started
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says the song was cut off. The song is in verse 11, and then the people give a great shout. What they couldn't do in verse 13 was distinguish the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping. The noise was just too much.
True. The text ends with it: "the sound was heard from afar." Joy and weeping together made enough noise to carry well beyond the foundation.
This one is True, friend. The last line of the passage says "the sound was heard from afar." That crowd was loud enough to be heard far from the temple foundation.
